turns.text: Hi. I need to talk to someone about something heavy—my thoughts and my body are kind of connected and it's getting really overwhelming.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm glad you reached out. I'm here to listen and help. What’s been weighing on you lately?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It's this constant noise. I used to have this voice that would whisper "I don't belong." It's gotten louder and I don't know how to shut it up.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds exhausting. When that voice is loudest, what do you notice in your body? And what thoughts pop up in those moments?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I get this weird numbness. Everything feels flat. I start thinking about not existing. I keep telling myself "no." I've even told people "no" to what I really want.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for sharing that. Are you feeling safe right now, and is there a plan or intention behind those thoughts, or is it more like "I wish I could stop existing" and the plan is just not planning anything?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don't want to hurt myself—like I used to—but recently I've been thinking about how I wish I could be dead. And I'm not making a plan. I just keep repeating "no" when I think about doing anything about it. I need help with this.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear you. I'm really glad you said that out loud. Are you somewhere safe right now? We can focus on getting you through the next few hours safely, and I can connect you with a crisis text line or urgent care if that helps.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm safe right now. I just feel like I'm stuck with this "I don't belong" voice and the body numbness. I keep saying "no" to everything that could help.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Okay. Let’s make it tiny and steady—can we pick one thing for today that’s even a little easier? Maybe slow breathing, a short walk, or texting someone you trust if you have a phone. Would that feel doable?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I can try breathing. I could also reach out to someone, but my brain just keeps looping "no" even when I want to.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That looping makes sense. How about we make a small contract: if the "no" thought shows up, pause, do one grounding thing (like naming 5 things you see, 4 you feel), then check in with me or text a line.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I can try that. Also, do you have any advice for that "I don't belong" voice—how to make it quiet?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Two quick ideas: 1) Name that voice as a separate person or part—you don’t have to believe it—and gently say, "I choose to stay with my body and breathe." 2) Practice “I am enough” statements. I can also refer you to therapy or support that focuses on body-based and thought-based patterns, and if you’d like, we can set up regular check-ins.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. Please help me with the plan—slow breathing, the grounding, and I'll text someone or you. I just want this constant noise to calm down, even for today.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: i'm so tired of being a mess. i don't wanna do this anymore. why can't i just feel okay?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm really glad you reached out. When you say "do this," what comes to mind—do you mean self-harm? And what's been going on that's making this feel so heavy?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: yeah. i've been cutting again. i can't stop, and i'm sick of the pain and the shame.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for telling me. I'm sorry you're hurting right now. Are you in immediate danger, and is anyone with you?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: i'm safe. it's just… i'm stuck in this loop. every time i try to stop, it's like i have to do it again.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes a lot of sense. Would you be open to making a plan for tonight—like keeping things you might use at distance, and setting a small, specific goal so the urge has a target?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: maybe. i'm just so tired and i feel like this is all i know.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Let's make it concrete. Pick one hour tonight and set a 10-minute window when you'll ride the wave. Options for the 10 minutes: hold ice, take a shower, draw on your skin with makeup, write, sip water, or do a grounding exercise. Pick a simple anchor for when the urge spikes.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: a 10-minute window sounds doable. maybe i can write while i take a cold shower.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That's a solid plan. If the urge intensifies, try the 10 minutes plus a grounding move (feet on the floor, name 5 things you see, 4 you feel, 3 you hear). We can also set a check-in for after you finish this hour.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: okay. if it gets worse, i'll try those grounding things and text you after.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm glad you're thinking about that. For support, you can also text 988 (the U.S. suicide and crisis lifeline) for immediate help if it feels overwhelming. You don't have to carry this alone.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: i'll try texting them if it spikes. i just feel like there has to be a way to stop.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: There is. Today, it's about getting through tonight and building small steps. I'm here with you right now, and I'll be checking in with you after the hour. You deserve to feel even a little better.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: okay. i'll start the shower and write, and i'll reach out when the hour is done. thank you for talking with me.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hey… can I ask something kinda personal? I’ve been thinking about this a lot lately, and it’s messing with my head.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Of course. I’m here to listen. What’s been weighing on you?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: So… I’m really into a guy and I really like him. I’ve got feelings for him. I really really like him. I think he’s nice and fun, and he’s not really my type. I feel like I might actually like him in a romantic sense, but I don’t feel in love with him. So I’m confused.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds really confusing. Does it feel like it’s a crush vs a deep connection? What’s the part that’s stumping you the most?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I feel like it’s more than a crush. I get to talk to him and I feel happy and relaxed, and I like spending time with him. He’s not like other guys I’ve dated, so I don’t really know if I’m in love with him or not.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Got it. When you say “not really my type,” what do you mean? And how long have you felt that way?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It’s more the “not in love” part. I just feel attached to him and maybe I want to get closer. I don’t want to say something and ruin anything.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear you. How do you see the relationship right now—friend, something more? And what’s one simple thing you can say if you do choose to say it?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don’t even know. I like being around him, and I want to know where we stand. Maybe I just need to ask or not say anything and let it unfold.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Totally fair. If you decide to ask, you could go super simple: “I like you a lot, and I want to know if you feel the same.” If you don’t want to say it, that’s okay too.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I keep thinking, am I in love with him? Or am I just comfortable around him because I like him? It feels like both at the same time.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That mix is real. Love isn’t just about type—it’s about what happens when you’re with them: connection, comfort, joy. You’re allowed to say you like them without calling it love yet.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, I want to tell him I like him, but I’m scared of saying the wrong thing. I just want to know where I stand with him.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: If you want, we can practice a few phrases together—short, clear, low-pressure. I can also help you notice what happens in the moment to see what you feel.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That would help. I just want to feel okay saying it, even if it’s just a small step.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: One idea: “I like talking to you, and I want to know if you feel the same.” Then check his response. If it helps, you could also send a quick “thanks for talking—I liked it,” to keep it light.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Thanks for listening. This helps a lot.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: hi. i just need to rant about this stupid "i can't take it" stuff. i've never been like that. i've never said i can't take the world or i can't take life. i've never even been on social media. i don't do memes, i hate memes, i hate social media, i've literally never said i can't take it. i just don't get why people are always saying that. i'm so tired of hearing it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm really glad you posted. That frustration makes a lot of sense. What do you wish people would hear or understand from your side?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: i just get tired of hearing it and i don't think i'm overreacting. i'm normal. i'm not saying i can't take anything. i don't say that about anything, i don't say i can't take this, i don't say i can't take that.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You're not being dramatic. A lot of people do use “i can't take it” in different contexts—like when they're overwhelmed or stressed. How does that show up for you? Is it comments, texts, or something in your own space?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: it's everywhere. people use that phrase a lot and it just bugs me. it's not a joke. it's real and it bugs me. i'm not a drama queen i'm just tired of it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s understandable. When you’re around it, what helps the most—talking it out, a break, or just letting it go for now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: i mostly just want people to stop saying it. i don't think i'm overreacting. i'm normal. i'm not saying i can't take anything.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Totally, you’re not overreacting. We can set boundaries and maybe find a way to share your thoughts without being pulled into that script.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: yeah. maybe i can tell people, “i’m fine. i’m not saying i can’t take it. i’m not a drama queen.” and then change the subject.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That could work. Short and firm. You could also ask them what’s making them say it, so it doesn’t feel like a punch to the gut.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: i don't even know if it's just people or if it's a meme thing. i don't do social media, i hate memes, and i've literally never said i can't take it. i'm just tired.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Meme culture does warp phrases and make them feel common. Your normal is valid, and you can choose how much you engage.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: i just want to be taken seriously. i'm not trying to get pity. i'm not saying i can't take it. i'm just tired of hearing people say it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear that. You can keep it simple: “i don’t say i can’t take it. i’m okay.” It’s okay to set boundaries. What would feel like the healthiest distance for you?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: i think i'll just say it when it comes up and move on. maybe i can also avoid social media for now so it's not on me.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi, I'm not sure how to ask. I'm in a really bad place with my mental health lately, and I keep wondering what the point is. I don't want to talk to anyone.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm glad you told me. I'm here to listen and help. What feels heaviest about it right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I can barely get out of bed most days. People tell me "you deserve happiness" but I feel so... empty. It's exhausting.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds really heavy. When it hits, what does it look like for you—thoughts, body, energy?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Days are bleak and nights are the worst. Everything feels pointless. I keep thinking, am I a waste?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear how much you're carrying. When that voice is loudest, do any little things—like a shower, a short walk, or a simple snack—help even a little?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Sometimes a shower, but usually I just feel too tired to do anything.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: We can make it tiny. How about we aim for one tiny thing that requires the least energy—like sitting up for 10 minutes or sipping water—just to keep the momentum going?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe 10 minutes sounds okay. The whole "point" thing still freaks me out.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Totally fair. Sometimes the point is about showing up today, not having the whole plan figured out. We can keep it simple for a few days—what feels most doable?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I could try one tiny thing—sit up 10 minutes. I don't want to be judged, but I don't know where else to vent.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You don't have to carry that alone. I'm here to hold it without judgment. I can check in with you on how that tiny step felt.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That helps. I just don't want to be told I "deserve" something. I don't feel worthy.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You're allowed to feel like that and still deserve care. Let's set a check-in for tomorrow and plan another tiny step—how does that sound?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. Tomorrow I'll try to sit up for 10 minutes and I'll check in. Thank you for not judging me.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm 22 and I just found out that my dad had a kid when he was 17. That's me, 17 years old at the time, and my dad had me at 17. How is that even possible?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That's a lot to take in. Do you have more details—like what led him to start the family, or how he felt about it back then?

turns.text: It's my brother. I'm 22 now, so he's 16. He's 5'10" and weighs 125, barely eats, and is extremely depressed. His mom took him and his little sister to live with another man. He never really saw his dad after that, and now I don't have a dad because he was too young to be a dad when my brother was born and then I was born.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm really sorry you're dealing with this. What has that been like for you as a brother, and what's your dad been telling you about what happened?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: He says it was because of me. He didn't want to be a father because I was going to be born and he was too young. That's just how it went down, and now my brother is 16 and he's got depression.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That kind of blaming can hurt so much. Are you two in contact with your dad, and is there anything you've been told about why he took your brother and sister in the first place?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah. It was his way of getting rid of him. He took my brother and his sister to live with another man, which caused a lot of problems. He was also the only one who could help them because my brother and sister don't have any other family.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds really painful. How are you feeling hearing all of this—shocked, sad, angry, or all of it?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Honestly, shocked. I don't even know if my dad knew my brother had a serious mental illness. He was just so young, and then my brother is 16 and barely eats and is extremely depressed.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s a lot to process. Would it help to talk to your brother about what’s happening so you can support each other, or would you want to talk to a therapist first?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Honestly I can't take this. I'm so confused and angry. Why was my brother born like this? Why is he so depressed? Who is his dad?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: It’s okay to feel that. If you can, write down what’s bothering you the most—facts and feelings—and we can break it down together. Would you be open to looking at a family therapist to help with the strain?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don't even know how to process this. I'm 22, and now I have a 16-year-old brother with serious depression, and our dad took him and his sister to live with another man.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m really sorry. Let’s try a few steps: 1) Write down exactly what you remember about your dad, his reasons, and how your brother ended up with another man. 2) If safe, reach out to him in a calm, neutral way and ask for what he remembers. 3) Check if your brother is getting any kind of support or care; if not, you can gently ask your dad or another adult to help. 4) If this feels overwhelming, look for counseling for you and your brother.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That makes a bit of sense. I don't want to blame anyone, but I want answers and someone who can help.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes sense. You deserve care and truth. Start with one small step—pick a time to ask him for the facts—and keep your eyes on your brother’s needs, too.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. I'll try to write it all down and think about how to talk to him.

turns.text: Hi, uh. I don't even know where to start. I'm kind of freaking out about something that happened a while ago and it's messing with me every day.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm glad you came in. We can go at your pace. What's been feeling the hardest?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds really painful. Are you feeling safe right now? And when you say "intense," what does that feel like day to day?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm really sorry you're dealing with that. If you want to share what he did, you can take as much time as you need. We can also focus on coping right now—what's been helping or helping the least?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm scared to say it because it's so painful. I don't even want to tell my mom. I know it wasn't the first time.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You don't have to share details you're not ready for. If it helps, you can stay general. Would you feel okay telling me it's about sexual abuse?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for trusting me. None of this is your fault. What parts of this feel the scariest—memories, triggers, or both?

turns.text: He raped me multiple times. I was a sexual abuse survivor before this relationship and I was still surviving then, but now I feel like I've lost the ability to survive and live.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm so sorry. What you're going through is extremely painful, and I'm here to help. Are you safe right now, and do you have any support or resources you're already using?

turns.text: I'm safe now. I just don't know how to move forward. I still love him and I miss him. He's not here and I'm not okay without him.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: It makes sense to feel that way, and you don't have to move forward on your own. We can work on coping tools, self-care, and rebuilding. Would you be open to a safety plan and a small step you can try this week?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, I can try a plan. I'm ready to start therapy and to not isolate myself anymore. Thank you for listening.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi… can I talk to you? I'm not feeling great and I don't really have anyone else to talk to.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Of course. I'm glad you reached out. What's been going on for you today?

turns.text: I just got back from the hospital for a blood test after getting really sick in the car. It was a rough morning with my dog, and he doesn't seem to understand me.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds exhausting. How is the sickness feeling right now—is it coming on in waves or is it steadying?

turns.speaker: User

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear you. What would help most—rest, water, food? And do you have anyone you could lean on tonight?

turns.text: A little rest would help. I don't know if I'll be up to anything tonight. With my dog I just feel like I'm doing the wrong thing, like he's judging me or something.

turns.text: It makes sense to feel like that after what you went through. Would it help if I check in again later to see how you're doing?

turns.text: Okay. We can plan a check-in. For now, try to keep your body supported—water, easy food, and try to rest while it steadies. How's the dog taking it?

turns.text: He's been acting kind of weird, like he doesn't understand me, and I keep feeling guilty. I'm just trying to calm down.

turns.text: I'm here with you. When your symptoms are steadier, maybe a short walk or gentle activity could help your system reset. For now, rest and gentle support are best.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That sounds good. I just want it to stop feeling so heavy tonight.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm here with you. If the heaviness spikes, text me or your hospital number—it's okay to ask for help when you need it.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Thanks. I'll try to rest and keep you posted. I just needed to talk for a bit tonight.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm really sorry you're going through this. Are you safe right now, and do you have anyone with you? How long has this been going on?

turns.text: Thank you for saying it. Are you thinking about ending your life tonight, and do you have any intention to do so right now?

turns.text: I'm here with you. Are you in the UK, and are you able to text or call emergency services right now? You could also message a crisis line like Samaritans (UK) to talk to someone while we wait.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You're doing the right thing. While you're texting, could you text or call someone you trust, like a friend, or use a safe messaging option if you're not sure? And if you're in bed, could you move to another room if it feels safer?

turns.text: I can move to the living room. I'm texting now. I'm scared but I'm trying.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That's brave of you. Keep texting 999 and Samaritans/your local line. If you're in a place with your phone on you, that helps. Keep talking here too. If it's possible, put distance between you and anything you could use to hurt yourself.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm texting them right now. I don't have a plan yet. I just wanted to say it out loud.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm so glad you told me. Keep chatting as you wait. You don't have to carry this alone. If someone replies, stay with them and keep talking.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi, I need to report something I saw a few days ago on campus that made me really uncomfortable.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for coming in. We’re here to help. Can you walk me through what happened in your own words?

turns.text: I was walking in a hallway at a local campus. I saw this man in his 50s, dressed in a black leather jacket and jeans, walking with a bottle of wine in hand. turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I understand. When you say it felt unsafe, what about the situation stood out to you most—his actions, the way they seemed private, or something else?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for describing that. Did you step in or did you go on your way, and what, if anything, happened after?

turns.text: I turned the other way. After a minute or so he pulled up to me, looked me dead in the eyes for about 20 seconds, and then he walked off and went back to his friend. I just stared at him in awe and then kept walking.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds like a scary and uncomfortable moment. We can document the location and what you saw. Would you be okay sharing a bit of detail about where you were, and if you noticed any ID or license plate, or if it’s from the campus area?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don’t need to identify myself. I was on campus, and it was a short hallway. I didn’t see ID or a license plate, but I saw him in a black leather jacket, jeans, holding a bottle of wine, and he had that same look he gave me that said he wanted to ask her something. I reported it because I feel like I should and I want to help.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I appreciate that. Are you physically okay now, and is there anything we should do to keep you safe in the meantime?

turns.speaker: Listener

turns.text: Hi, I don't usually come to these kinds of places but I really needed to talk. I'm in the UK and I have this new job I love, but the only coworker is a total jerk. He's been bullying me. He told my manager he had my back and that I was stupid, and now I'm the only person who works with him. I'm so stressed. Any advice?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm really sorry you're going through this. That sounds overwhelming. What part of it feels the heaviest day to day—his comments, the pressure from your manager, or not having your coworkers on your side?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: All of it honestly. He constantly belittles me and tells my manager he has my back. I feel set up and not trusted. I have this new job I love but I just can't handle it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s a lot to carry. You deserve respect. What does the bullying look like in your day-to-day and how often has this been going on?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It’s all in my head and at work. He’s the only person in the office and I’m just a regular coworker. We get along, but he keeps saying I’m stupid, and it’s been going on for weeks.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thanks for sharing that. Do you have any documentation, screenshots, emails, or messages from him? And does he do that on company property or on a work system you can save?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It’s mostly just verbal at work and then he tells my manager he’s got my back. I can save any messages or emails he sends me, but it’s just a few comments.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Okay. You could start by saving all communication and keeping a log of when and what he says. Then, in a low-pressure moment, you might request a private meeting with your manager to clarify expectations and set boundaries, and ask how you’re supposed to handle this if he doesn’t stop. Have you tried that yet?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I haven’t brought it up yet. I’m scared I’ll be seen as a complainer or something.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Totally fair to feel that. You can keep it factual and neutral. For example, “I need clear boundaries around our communication so I can do my job without being harassed.” If you don’t have a workplace policy on bullying or verbal abuse, then bringing it to HR or the HR representative is a solid next step. How does that feel?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It still feels risky to open that door, but I know I have to do something. I just don’t want it to ruin this new job.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You don’t have to make it about “ruining” the job. Your well-being matters. You could also consider limiting one-on-one time with him when possible and, if you can, request a different colleague or team to work with. In the meantime, set up boundaries like not responding to his negativity and keeping conversations task-focused.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’m still nervous. I’ve never had to deal with this before.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear you. You could start small: draft the email, practice the wording, and send it when you’re calm. If the manager isn’t clear or supportive, escalating to HR or an external HR rep is a strong move. And if you’re in the UK, there’s the Equality and Human Rights Commission’s guidance for workplace issues—worth checking out.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Thanks. I’ll start by saving the messages, draft an email to my manager, and keep a log. I’ll look into the HR part too. Appreciate the advice and the support.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi. I don’t even know what to say. I just need to be heard.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You’re heard. What’s been going on?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It’s my dad, he’s super controlling. My mom is super quiet. He does all the shopping, and she doesn’t say much.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds really heavy. What does it feel like for you in the house?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I always feel like the bad kid. I’m not doing anything, he doesn’t see me. He doesn’t even ask about my day. He just looks at me like I’m annoying.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s a lot to carry. How are you doing day to day—sleep, school, anything that’s been hard?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Honestly I don’t know. It feels like I’m just invisible.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: When he calls you a “bad kid,” how does that hit you? Are you in school right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, I’m in high school. I get called that a lot. I just want a friend or something to talk to.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m glad you came to me. Would it feel okay to try one small step—like one person at school or one message to a friend you already know?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe. I’m not sure who to reach out to. My dad doesn’t even talk to me.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You could start with someone you know from class or a club. I can help you draft something simple, and we can pick one person to try first.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. Maybe I’ll send a short message or say hi to someone today.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m proud of you. If it feels okay, we can set up a check-in so you don’t feel alone. And if something about home is really pressing, we can talk about options too.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Thanks. I just needed someone to listen, really. I’ll try talking to one person.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’m 17 and I want to drop out of high school. I don’t really have any friends there, my parents don’t really support it, and I really don’t like the school. I’m scared to even talk about it to them because of the consequences, and I don’t have anyone else to talk to. I’m just looking for any advice or suggestions.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds really overwhelming. When you say you don’t like the school, what’s been the hardest part for you day to day?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Mostly that I’m not making any friends and I don’t really want to go back every day. It feels pointless.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Totally fair. When you think about what you want, is it more about a better fit, less stress, or something else?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Better fit, I guess. I just don’t fit in. I feel like I’m wasting my time.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes sense. Do you have any teachers or staff you can talk to about options, or do you feel too embarrassed to ask?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, I’m embarrassed. If I ask about dropping out, will they just say no?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: They’re there to help you understand options. You could also check your school’s website for info about alternative education paths, like a dual enrollment program or a local online program.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’ve heard of some options but I don’t know where to start.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Try a quick search for “dual enrollment [your state]” or “online high school program.” Also, a school counselor or a guidance office might have someone who can guide you through the process.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Even if my parents don’t support it, can I still do something without making it a huge deal? I’m scared to tell them.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You can try a low-pressure option first. For example: “Hey, I’m looking into dual enrollment and online options this summer. What do you think?” If they push back, you can add, “I just want to try something different and see if I can find a fit.”

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe. They’re pretty strict about school, though. I don’t want a big fight.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Totally fair. A small step might be best: look up and apply for one program, then come back and see if they’d support it. You can also keep your grades strong so you have options later.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That helps. I’ll try looking at online/dual enrollment options and see what fits, and maybe have a short talk with the school counselor. Thanks for not making me feel dumb.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi, I’m here because I’m stuck figuring out how to handle something at home. My ex-wife is trying to contact me again and I don’t know what to do.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m glad you came in. Can you tell me what’s been going on and what you’ve been seeing from her lately?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It’s like she’s trying to get back in. She called and messaged me, and now we’re having a back-and-forth on Facebook. We’re both friends, but it feels like she wants to drag me back in.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds confusing and concerning. How has this made you feel lately—safe? uneasy? and what does it feel like she wants from you?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Honestly I’m nervous. I told her we’re done and I don’t want her back, but she keeps bringing stuff up. And this back-and-forth is making me feel like I should at least talk to her.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for sharing that. When you say “at least talk,” how would you feel if you actually did talk to her today? Would you be safe in the moment?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I keep telling myself I should just ignore her, but the way she talks and starts these little back-and-forth conversations worries me. I don’t know what to do.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear how worried you are. To help, could you share a bit about why you left and what the safety concerns have been for you?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: She was very abusive to me. I’m so much happier now since we’re not together, and I’m trying to move on.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for trusting us with that. When you say “abusive,” what kind of behavior have you dealt with that makes you feel unsafe?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It was ongoing. She pushed, insulted me daily, called me names, and physically abused me. I was scared all the time when she was around. I left and it felt good not to be around her, but now she keeps coming back and I’m not sure if she’ll try to push me back.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m so sorry you went through that. You deserve safety. Would you like a plan for how to set clear boundaries while she’s reaching out? We can also document her attempts and connect you with DV services for support.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yes, I want a plan. I want to tell her I’m not talking and that I’m done.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Okay—start a simple message like, “I’m done. I won’t be talking to you or coming back.” Avoid agreeing to meetings or “friend” requests. Turn off notifications, block her, and save copies of your messages. Would you like me to help you draft those words?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yes, please. And remind me not to respond to anything she sends. I want it to stop.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: We can. For immediate safety, if there’s any chance she could try to contact you again, consider telling a trusted friend, your manager, or a local shelter. We’ll also connect you with DV advocates and counseling so you have ongoing support.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Thank you. I’m going to send that message now, block her, and reach out to the DV hotline. I just needed someone to tell me I’m not crazy for not wanting to talk.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I keep thinking I shouldn’t feel this way, but I’m scared of my life without the scars.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m really glad you posted. I care about you and I want to listen. What’s been going on with you, and how are you feeling today?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It’s been months since I was stabbed, and I still hate that I’m missing my own self-made scars.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds really painful. Are you safe right now, and would you be open to talking about what happened and what you’re dealing with day to day?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I self harm and it’s been a while since I got stabbed. I still miss the scars from self harming.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for telling me. I’m so sorry you’re going through this. Are you hurt now, and do you need medical care today? You’re not alone, and I want to support you.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’m not dying. I’m okay. I just feel lost and scared to live without the scars I made. They were my only connection to me.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear how much that means to you. You don’t have to go through this alone. Would it help to focus on getting through today and finding other ways to cope when urges hit?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, I can get through today. I just don’t know how to fill that void. I used to use self harm as a way to feel something, and now it’s just empty.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes a lot of sense. When urges show up, you could try grounding—cold water on your wrists, holding ice, holding something heavy. We can also make a small plan: a grounding exercise and someone to message if it spikes.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe. It still feels weird without the scars, though. I keep comparing myself to how I was before.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Comparison can make it worse. If you want, we can work on replacing the urge with other ways to feel noticed and cared for—writing, talking to someone you trust, or a short walk. How does that sound?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Writing might help. I can try a note or drawing. I just needed to say it out loud.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s exactly what I wanted you to say. You matter, and your life still has value. If you need extra support tonight, you could message me or reach out to someone you trust.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. I’ll try the grounding and a short walk and a note tonight. Thanks for talking to me.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m here. If anything changes or you need medical care, please message me. Take it one step at a time—cold water on your wrists, hold something heavy, and remind yourself you’re not alone.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. I’ll do that. Thank you.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hey. I need to vent. I left my abusive ex a few months ago, and I still feel guilty about it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm glad you came in. What's been making the guilt stick the most?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I told myself I was staying for his kids, that I could be the calm one for them and I could love them too. I never imagined I'd leave him, but I did.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds incredibly painful. Were you in immediate danger when you left?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: We were in my car. The kids were asleep. We weren't doing anything dangerous. He kept pushing me to stay.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for sharing that. When you say "abusive," what kind of abuse have you been dealing with?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm a DV survivor and I left him because of domestic abuse.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm sorry that happened. I'm glad you told me. Are you safe now, and is anyone still contacting you?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, I'm safe now. We're still together, he didn't do anything that night, and I can't stand to see him with the kids. I keep questioning myself.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Leaving an abusive relationship is a huge step. You chose yourself and safety. When the guilt hits, what thoughts show up?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I keep telling myself, "You were there for his kids." I feel like I failed them. He says it was my fault.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Those are powerful, unfair messages, but they're not true. You did what you needed to. Would you be open to some grounding for the "I failed them" thoughts?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, I want something to counter the guilt. I just want it to stop.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: How about we write a short statement for yourself: "I chose safety. I did what I had to do." Repeat it when the guilt spikes, and name a few moments you did care for the kids. Would that help?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That could help. I just need it to stop feeling like I made it worse.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi. Can I talk about something that makes me feel a bit sick. I'm 24 and I have no friends, and I just don't know why that is.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Of course. I'm glad you came in. What have you been noticing about your social life, and are you finding it hard to make new friends?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Most people don't know my name or even who I am. If I make a post I don't get a lot of attention, and it gets worse with my older friends.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds really discouraging. Do you think it's more the posts, or more the connections you're trying to build with people?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Honestly it's both. And honestly, it's just frustrating. I feel invisible.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That frustration makes sense. What’s the last time you tried to start something new—like a group, event, or online community—would you say it felt hard or easy?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: The last time I tried to start something new was… I don’t even remember. It just feels like I never start anything.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Got it. Sometimes starting a new thing can feel scary. Would you be open to trying tiny steps—like one tiny step, no pressure?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe one small step, yeah. I'm just not sure where to start.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Totally okay. Let’s keep it low pressure. Options: 1) Try a 10-minute check-in post with an open question; 2) Send a short, low-pressure message to someone; 3) Join a single group online this week and log one thing you noticed. Which feels least scary?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe the 10-minute check-in post with an open question. I can try that.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Great. For the post, keep it simple: “Hey all—what’s been going on this week?” No pressure to comment. You could also reply to a couple of comments just once a week to keep it low stress.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I like the simple thing. And I could try a couple replies. It just feels so lonely sometimes.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Loneliness is real, and we can work on that together. We’ll check in again, and you’ll get an email reminder if you want. If it gets heavier, we’ll also talk about supports to help you feel less invisible.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. I think that’s a good plan—tiny step with the post and a couple replies, and I’ll check in again.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: My sister's a drug dealer, and I’m scared. Every time he shows up, he’s got a gun and he yells at her and the little kids like it’s nothing. I’m 10 years old and I’m scared. He even took her little cousin hostage a few times. I feel so small and scared.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m really sorry you’re going through this. Are you safe to talk right now? I can’t help with anything illegal, but I want to hear you and help you keep yourself and your family safe.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: We’re safe to talk. He only comes around when there’s a lot of money, and he doesn’t like people leaving. I’ve seen him threaten to shoot her if we tried to leave with money. I told my mom and my little cousin. I don’t know what to do.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for telling me. If he ever shows up, what happens—do people stay quiet, or can anyone leave? Has your mom been able to get out of the house? And have you and your cousin had a plan if it gets rough?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: He shows up when there’s lots of money, he yells, and the kids just take it. Sometimes he even takes the little cousin hostage. I’m scared and feel tiny. I don’t want her to get hurt.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s terrifying. If he shows up, you and your cousin could try to go outside and tell someone—call the police or a local center, or maybe reach a neighbor. If you can’t go outside, stay inside and keep your phone charged and ready. Your mom can stay calm and keep the door closed if he starts with her.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’ve told my mom and cousin. I’m scared, and I feel so small. He even said if we tried to leave he’d shoot her. I don’t know what to do.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You didn’t do anything wrong. You did the right thing by telling an adult. Keep it simple: stay safe, keep your phone charged, and tell someone as soon as you can. Avoid fighting or confrontation. If you’re in the U.S., you can call a local police nonemergency line; in other places, find the equivalent local line or call emergency. If you can, write a short message like “I’m scared. I need help.”

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’m 10 and I don’t know how to do this without my parents or my cousin. I feel tiny and scared.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You’re not tiny. You’re doing what you can. You can text someone you trust or a local hotline. If you can, write the message and put it in your pocket. If you can’t leave the room, stay quiet and keep your phone ready. If you can, get outside to a neighbor’s or call the police nonemergency.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. I can write a message and keep my phone ready. I don’t want my little cousin to get hurt.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you. If the situation escalates and someone gets hurt, please call emergency. Right now, focus on staying safe and trying to contact someone you trust or a local police. I’m here to help you get through this.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I told my cousin and mom already, and I don’t want them getting hurt. I just need to stay safe and keep my phone charged.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s exactly right. Keep your phone nearby, write a short message, and find the safest way to send it. Keep your voice steady and try to leave if you can. We can check in after you’ve sent the message—would that be okay?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, after I send the message I can send you a quick note. Please stay on so I can talk to you again.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I've been on my own for a month, and I'm still dealing with the aftereffects from my ex.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm glad you reached out. What's been the hardest part since you moved out?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Sleep. He never let me sleep at night, and now my head's buzzing. I feel like I'm just waiting to be attacked again.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That constant hypervigilance is really tough. Have you noticed any physical reactions like a pounding heart or shaky hands?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah. My heart won't stop racing, my hands shake, and I don't know what to do with myself.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear you. Would you be open to some practical steps and support to help with sleep and the anxiety spike? When you notice the panic, how does it hit?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. I was in an abusive relationship—he’d beat me. I moved out a month ago, and now it’s still in my head.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for trusting us with that. Are you safe right now, and do you have any medical concerns that need urgent attention?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm safe now. No medical stuff. It's more about this constant fear and the sleep stuff.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Got it. For sleep: try a consistent wind-down—no screens for 45–60 minutes, a warm shower, light snack, and a calming activity. When panic hits, can you try 6–10 breaths, ground on 5 senses, and step outside if you can?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I can try the shower and a warm drink and maybe some quiet music. The breath thing sounds doable.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Good. For after-hours, consider text support if it helps—many places offer 24/7. If the shakes get too much, can you keep lights on or put something on the nightstand you can grip? And I can connect you with a counselor who specializes in trauma.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, a counselor would help. A hotline could help too. What else can I do to stop this loop?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm glad you're reaching out. A short therapy-focused course or self-help plan might help, and grounding skills can lower the spiral. If things get worse or you're worried you're not healing, I can adjust the plan or refer to inpatient care.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Thank you. I'm going to try the steps, use the hotline if I need it, and check in with you so I can get some guidance.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm 19 and have been working a night shift for a bit. I'm exhausted and I'm trying to decide whether to keep it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm glad you told me. How long have you been doing it, and what’s been weighing on you most?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe 2–3 months now. It’s a good paycheck, but I’m sleep-deprived and it’s messing with my mental health. I’m not sure I can keep going.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds tough. When you say it’s messing with your mental health, what does that feel like day to day?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’m so tired and irritable. My brain doesn’t switch off at night. I feel run down. I’m worried about long-term health too.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes a lot of sense. What would you need to make a decision that helps you feel okay?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: More sleep, maybe a less demanding schedule, or some stability. Right now I just want to not feel so wrecked all the time.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: We can aim for both. Do you have anyone at work you could talk to about a more flexible schedule or fewer hours, or would it be easier to step back first?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I could try asking about fewer hours if there’s room. I’m also thinking about what happens if I leave—could I get a different job with regular hours or less wear on me?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Those are solid questions. Do you have people who can support you with a job search while you transition, or do you want to talk through what options feel possible?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don’t have a huge support system yet, but I’m open to learning what’s possible. Maybe I can start small—less hours here and look into other places.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds thoughtful. Would you want to write down a couple of priorities and steps to keep moving forward?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, maybe: 1) Ask my manager about fewer hours, 2) Set a goal to get more sleep/less exhaustion, 3) Look into part-time or daytime jobs, and 4) Plan for how I’ll handle income until I land something.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s a clear path. I can help you practice talking to your manager and we can look at job resources together. Would you want me to sit with you through an email or a meeting?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That would help. Thank you. I just needed someone to help me think through how to keep my head about this.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm in the middle of a therapy session and it just hit me. My therapist mentioned that the abuse I endured when I was 10 is not that extreme, but that doesn't feel true to me.

turns.speaker: Listener
