turns.text: She took one donut, the other one was already eaten, then she left. She said nothing. It was really awkward and I felt bad and confused.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear you. When she looked at you like she knew—did she look like she was judging you? Does that kind of thing usually make you freeze?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, she looked like she knew. I felt like I’d done something wrong even though I just wanted to be nice. She ate one donut, and I felt like a creep.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You wanted to be nice, and you did. If it helps, you didn’t do anything wrong. Sometimes people see kindness and assume it’s a joke or they’re being judged, and their eyes do that kind of “dead” thing. What do you wish you’d said or done after?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Honestly I froze. I kept thinking I’d done something wrong. I still kind of feel like I did, even though I just wanted to do something nice.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: It makes sense to feel that way. If you want, you can talk it through with the person or just write it off as a weird coincidence. What matters is that you acted with good intent.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I think I just need someone to validate it—like yeah, it was nice and I didn’t do anything wrong.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m validating it. You were nice. Her reaction was hers, not yours.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. I’m still nervous about how she took one donut and left like that.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Maybe it’s a story that’ll fade. If it’s still rattling you, a quick text like “Hey, what happened at that coffee shop?” could help, but it’s up to you.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Thank you. I appreciate the support. I’ll try to just let it go.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I've been thinking a lot about that night and I'm kind of freaking out. I feel like it's gonna ruin my whole life.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm glad you posted. What happened, and how is it showing up for you right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm 19 and my boyfriend is 30. Our relationship isn't perfect, but he's my first boyfriend and I don't want to end it. I don't want to feel this way forever.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds really conflicting. What about that night feels like the breaking point?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It was the first time we slept together. I was nervous but also excited, and then we started talking about sex after. We were making it up as we went along, and it felt off. I felt like I didn't like him that much. He didn't want me to say no, so I just went with it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds intense and confusing. When did the feeling about that night start coming up again?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: A few weeks ago he asked if I've ever had sex with someone before and I said no, and then he asked if he's my first, and I said yes. It felt weird because I know it wasn't perfect and we were just trying to figure it out together. He also asked about my sexual history, and I felt like I had to answer because I felt bad. I told him I wasn't a virgin.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Telling someone you're not a virgin after the first time can be hard. What does that make you feel in the moment and afterward?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Guilty and stupid. Like I ruined the first time. Like I did something wrong. And he told me it's okay to be a virgin, but I wasn't, so I'm just like, nope, it still ruined it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That self-blame is common after sex and especially after a difficult first time. What's been the hardest part of the guilt—how people see it or how it's affecting your head right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: The hardest part is that it wasn't even the first time for me. I've been raped before, and I was raped again, and then my mother took me to the hospital and the guy who raped me was arrested. But I'm still being blamed for what happened to me.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm really sorry that happened to you, and I'm sorry your mom had to do that. You are not to blame. If it feels right, you could choose to say what you want about past trauma to him—how it's affected how you view sex and consent, and that it's why you're being careful now.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I want to stop feeling so guilty and stop letting it define my life. I don't want to feel like I messed everything up forever.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes sense. One approach is to name the trauma as past and not connected to this relationship, and to focus on what matters now—mutual consent, respect, and trust. You could say something like, "I'm not comfortable with the idea of having a sexual relationship until I'm ready, and I'm trying to find that balance."

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I keep telling myself I ruined my first time and now I'm ruined forever. He says it's okay to be a virgin, but I wasn't, so I'm like nope, it still ruined it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: It's a hard truth that trauma can affect how you view sex and your body, and that doesn't make you less worthy of a caring relationship. For this relationship to work, you can focus on boundaries, clear consent, and care—what you want and need in the moment.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Thank you. I just need to feel less guilty and stop letting that night ruin the rest of my life.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi. Is it okay to vent a bit? Today was rough.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Of course. We can talk. What happened that made it rough today?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I was at a cafe with a friend. I didn’t know it was her birthday, so I brought her a tiny candle, a little chocolate. She started crying. I felt awful, I thought I ruined it for her.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds really painful. What made it hit you that hard?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I was so excited to give her a birthday gift, just because, and I thought it was kind. She’s going to be 30 and I’m jealous of that age.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: It makes sense you’d feel that way. Do you want to name the jealousy piece, or just vent the moment?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Both. I was just jealous of her birthday. Then she started crying and I thought I ruined it for her and now I feel bad about feeling jealous.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Feeling jealous is a normal human response. We can be kind to you about it, too. Would you want advice on that?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah. Also, I want to know what’s wrong with me. Is it okay to be jealous?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Feeling jealous is okay—it shows you care about that friend and maybe have goals for yourself. It’s not about what’s “wrong” with you. How would you like to handle it, in small ways?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don’t even know. I feel bad for feeling jealous of her birthday and then I feel bad for making her cry.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Two separate things: a feeling you can soften, and a mistake you can apologize for. What would a gentle apology look like?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe a simple I’m sorry for the tiny candle and chocolate, I didn’t mean to make it a big deal. I just wanted to do something nice.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s kind. And for the jealousy piece—maybe a check-in with yourself: what does that age mean to you, and what would help you feel closer to it?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe I’m scared of getting old and just feeling sad for her getting older. I don’t want to be that old.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That fear is valid. You could try a small plan for your 30th—save a little each month, or pick a project, or make a list of things you love about your current age—and revisit it when the urge hits.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I like that idea. And for her, maybe a simple “I’m glad you’re happy” or “I’ll still buy you a candle” next time.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Nice. If the jealousy comes up again, name it, then do one small step you’re proud of—kindness or self-care—so it doesn’t spiral.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Thanks. That helps. I’ll write down a small plan and try to be gentler with myself.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hello. I'm here because I cut myself again and I'm worried about a cut on my arm.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for coming in. I'm glad you're here. When did the cut happen, and does it hurt or bleed much right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It's a pretty deep cut. I think it's from the same thing that caused the rest of them. It's a bit hard to explain.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: We can take care of the wound safely. I want to make sure we address the whole area. Can you tell me how many of the other cuts you have and how old they are?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: There are over 20 cuts, most of them are around 10 days old. One is almost healed. This new one is about 4 days old—probably from the same thing I used before.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear you. It's important we talk about what's been happening, not just the injuries. Are you safe right now—no imminent danger?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm safe right now. It's more that I'm worried about the new one and the ones that are older—what if they get infected or something?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: We can clean and dress the wound, and I'll check the other cuts for signs of infection. Would you be open to also talking about the reasons you're cutting and how you're doing with urges?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah. I know I shouldn't do it, but it's been happening a lot lately and it scares me.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for saying that. Today we'll focus on your safety, wound care, and support. Would you be willing to try a plan for the next few days—like not cutting, keeping wounds clean, and getting through the urges with healthier choices?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I can try not to cut. It's just that the urges are really strong when they hit, and I'm scared the infection will be worse if they get worse.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes sense. For the infection risk, we'll make sure each cut is clean and dressed, and I'll show you how to care for it at home. If any turn red, hot, swollen, or you feel feverish, come back or call us. We can also connect you with therapy or support groups if that feels right.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don't know how to tell which ones are infected. It's hard to remember exactly where they are.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: We'll go through each cut, check for redness, warmth, pus, or pain, and dress them. I'll also give you written care steps. Between now and your next visit, if the urge spikes, we can make a short plan—like distracting, grounding, reaching out for support, or even stepping away from where you usually do this.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. I can try that plan and clean everything carefully. What should I avoid?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Avoid picking at scabs or scrubbing, use clean gloves if you have them, keep your hands away from the wounds, and don't use anything that could make it worse. Also, if the urge feels overwhelming, call or visit us—we can help you get through it.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi. I have a lot of anxiety and panic attacks, but I also have a pretty strong, stable job and a supportive partner. I just want to be more confident. I feel like I'm not getting anything right.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm glad you came in. That sounds like a lot of pressure on top of what's already hard. What parts feel heaviest day to day—work, home, relationships?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Honestly work. My boss keeps giving me these tiny projects and then I feel like I'm not doing enough. I'm tired and stressed.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That can wear you down. What’s a “tiny project” look like to you—how long, how much detail, and what do you usually end up doing with it?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: They're like… one or two days of work and I end up doing it. Then I feel like I'm just doing busy work instead of real work, and I'm drained.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Makes sense. Do you have any control over how he assigns work, or any way to talk with him about how things go?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don’t. It feels like I have to ask for feedback, and I usually do, and he just says he’ll keep me updated or it’s not my problem.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Okay. What would a “good” check-in look like to you—something short and clear?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe a quick “how are you doing?” or “anything I can help with?” I just don’t want to feel like I’m constantly asking.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Totally reasonable. Would you be open to suggesting a structured check-in—like sending it by email or calendar—and setting a cadence?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I could try email. I’m just nervous he’ll think I’m a problem.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You can frame it as a collaboration: “Hey, can I check in on the updates and ask if there are other priorities to focus on?” You might even say you’re balancing work and wellness.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, that feels more like asking for help than sounding like a complainer. How do I not overdo it?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I recommend one check-in a week and one brief weekly update. You can also set a limit on how many projects you commit to at once. Would you try that this week?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah. And I can write a simple email asking for feedback and clarity—no more than a couple lines.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Great. Let’s set it for Tuesday and send it. If that helps, we can also look at some low-stakes confidence-building outside work—like a weekly routine or journaling.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I need to tell you something that's been haunting me. It's about my ex, who was really abusive to me. I'm not ready to talk to anyone else about it yet.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm really glad you told me. What feels heaviest about it right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It's the night I left. I had been planning to call my mom and go to my mom's for the first time in months. I went to the store, got everything packed, and was about to leave when he caught me. He grabbed my keys, started arguing, and in that moment, I knew he'd never let me go.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s a terrifying moment. How did he hurt you that night, and how are you feeling in your body now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: He shoved me against the fridge and choked me—my face turned purple and I passed out. When I woke up, I was on the floor, and he was still on top of me, trying to convince me to stay. I couldn't breathe and my chest hurt.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for saying that. You’re not alone here. When he said you were “a stupid, broken woman,” what did that do to you, and what are you holding onto most from the past few years?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: He kept saying I was a stupid, broken woman, and he said he’d kill me. Those words stuck with me. I’ve tried to get over it and I’m still stuck—part of me just wants him to be punished for what he did.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Those thoughts make sense, especially when you’re in pain. You don’t have to have all the answers right now. When you think about the next few weeks, what would help you feel just a little safer—like a boundary you can set or someone you can talk to without judgment?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I just don’t want to relive it. I need space and a way to stop my brain from spiraling.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: We can keep this here. Would you want to set up a simple safety plan, like a code word you can use if things get tense, or identifying a person you can contact if you feel unsafe?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah. A simple plan would help. I’m still trying to move on and I need the support.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Good. How about we start with three low-effort steps: a grounding practice you can do when memories pop up, a code word with a trusted person, and one small step toward a hobby or routine that gives you control.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That sounds doable. I can practice the grounding and use a code word I can message.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m here for that. We’ll check in next time and adjust. If anything feels unsafe or unbearable, please contact your local crisis line or a local domestic violence hotline—your safety matters most.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Thank you. I’m grateful you’re listening and I’m going to try those steps.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi. I don’t even know what to say—this is kinda embarrassing, but I need to know if this is something I should be worried about.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You came in the right place. Can you tell me what’s been going on, and what part feels the most concerning?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay, it’s about self-harm—my arms. I’ve been cutting there, and I’m not sure if I’m doing it right or if it’s too much.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for saying that clearly. When did this start, and what usually sets it off? And can you share what you’re using and how deep you’re going with it?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It started about a month ago. It’s stress and I want a rush, so I go for it. I use an old blade from my knife set, I’ve only done it on my arms. I don’t really go super deep, but I’m still new and I’m scared I’m doing it wrong.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: We’re all about your safety. First, are any of these wounds still fresh, are you bleeding, or needing medical care? And do you notice any signs of infection—redness, heat, pus, a bad smell, fever?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Not infected that I can see. They’re mostly fresh but not bleeding a lot, and I’m not going to make them worse. It’s more the “is this wrong” part that’s worrying me.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Got it. We can’t advise you on what to cut, but I can help you set up safer boundaries and support. Has anyone helped you through this, or do you do this alone? And how often are you doing it?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I do it alone, mostly when I’m stressed. It’s not like I’m doing it every day, but when it spikes I lose myself.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes sense. To keep you safe: use a single-use blade only when you’re absolutely sure, keep it away from where you keep your knife set, plan a 24-hour “no cutting” stretch, and set a check-in with me. Would you be willing to make a simple safety plan for tonight?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, I can try. I don’t want to get hurt, and I’m just… scared it’s too much.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Your safety is the priority. For tonight: put the blade somewhere out of reach, drink some water, take a shower, write down what stress is hitting, and reach out to someone you trust if it gets intense. If anything changes, come back or text us.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. I can put the blade away and try not to do it tonight. I’m still worried about the depth and whether I’m making it worse.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: If you ever need a quick safety check while you’re out, we can do a remote consult—call or text, then come in if you need stitches. For now, stay on the plan, keep checking in with us, and consider therapy if you’re up for it. You’re not alone with this.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Thank you. I’ll try the plan tonight and message you if things spike. I just needed to know I’m not doing it wrong.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hey, do you mind if I talk to you about something heavy? I can't figure out how to ask my mom, and I really need someone to hear me.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm here. You can tell me anything. Are you safe right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, I'm safe. It's more like I'm stuck on something and I don't want to mess with family stuff.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Okay. When you say “something,” you can say it in your own words. What’s been pressing on you?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I've been having this urge for weeks—like dying is the only thing I want to focus on. It's not something I can ignore and I'm not making it up. I'm 20 years old and I want to end it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for saying that so clearly. I'm really glad you reached out. Are you in immediate danger right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Not right now. It's more like a constant thought. I'm in the U.S., and I don't know if I should just keep talking to you or if I should reach out to someone else.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You're doing the right thing by talking. In the U.S., you can text or chat with 988 anytime. We can also set up regular check-ins here, and if you can, tell your mom you need help without forcing details.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Texting sounds less intense. I just don't want to freak her out with the details.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes sense. You can say: “I'm not okay and I need help. Can you stay with me?” If it helps, we can practice a short message here.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. I'll try. I just keep thinking I want to die every day and it's not a passing thought.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds overwhelming, and it matters that it's persistent. For tonight, can you put distance between you and anything you could use to hurt yourself, and plan to reach out to 988 or me by morning?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I can put space between me and stuff. I can try texting 988 and you in the morning too.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Good plan. If the urge ramps up, you can message me right away, or use a crisis chat. We can also check in later today to see how you're doing.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Thanks. I'll text 988 and message you, and I'll try talking to my mom about it.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm trying to figure out if it was worth it. I was kind, I did the right things, I did the right things, and then I was betrayed, and now it feels like my whole life has been a waste.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm really sorry you're feeling this way. What did you try to do, and how did the betrayal feel in the moment?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I gave everything to my family, I was kind, I did the right things, I did the right things, and then I was betrayed. It feels like I just gave my life away to people I thought I could trust.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That hurts. How did you handle it after—what support did you reach out to, and what did you find hardest?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I reached out to my support system and started counseling. I told them what happened, and now I'm just stuck here feeling like nothing's helping.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: It makes sense to feel stuck. Do you have anyone who's been steady for you, even a little? And when you think about your family, what feelings come up right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don't really have family to turn to. I feel like the only one left to carry on is me. I'm tired, and I feel like I'm the only one who doesn't get it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s a heavy burden. You don’t have to bear it alone. Would you be open to a small step—like one person to talk to, or something that helps you feel a bit steadier day to day?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe. I just feel like nothing’s changed, and it makes me think maybe I should’ve never given my life away to people I thought I could trust.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: It sounds like the betrayal hit hard, and those feelings are real. What would feel like the smallest win to you—just 1% progress?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Honestly, even just getting out of bed without crying is a win. But the past makes me feel like it’s all just wasted.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: It’s okay for past pain to still show up, even if it’s not the whole story. You did what you did, and you can honor that while you take steps forward.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I do know what I did. I just feel like it’s all gone in circles.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: We can make it less circular. You could write down what happened in your own words, identify one person to be gentle with, and set one tiny routine that helps you reset each day—something like a 5-minute stretch, a walk, or journaling.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I can try that. A 5-minute routine and one person to reach out to. Maybe I can write it all down.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s a solid start. How about tonight: jot down what happened, note one person you could contact, and write one short message you’d send to yourself today?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. I’ll try tonight—write it out, find one person, and send a little message to myself. Thanks for listening.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’m so stressed with work, and I’ve been wanting to take a break for days. I’m just trying to get through this week.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m sorry you’re feeling this way. What’s making work feel the heaviest, and how have you been coping lately?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Honestly? It’s my head. I’ve been cutting so much, and even with all those scars, I still feel this constant need to cut.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for telling me directly. I’m really glad you reached out. When does the urge hit the hardest, and are you safe right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Mostly nights and weekends, but I still do it midday too. The urge is there all the time, even when it doesn’t hurt. My scars remind me how long I’ve done this.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds exhausting. Would you be open to making a small safety plan for tonight and next few days—things that can ride the urge out without putting you in danger?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I hate that I still need it. It feels stupid, like I shouldn’t have to hurt myself to feel normal.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear you. You’re not stupid. Your feelings are real. Sometimes we can build a buffer between the urge and the action—like putting distance between you and anything you could use, having distractions, or calling me if it gets overwhelming.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, I could keep things out of reach. I can try some of the stuff you suggested when it spikes.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Great. Could we also think about what’s going on at work that’s been building up? And do you feel supported by your coworkers?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’m doing my best, but I’m not okay. My brain won’t stop. I’m just trying to get through this week.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s a lot to carry. We can lower the bar and take it day by day. We can set a boundary around “no more” and check in with each other after this week. How does that sound?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It does sound good. I just want it to stop.

turns.speaker: Listener

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: it stayed the same for a long time. i’m 23 now and i started cutting in college when i was really young—like 18 and 19—and i stopped for a while.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Okay. When you say you “stopped,” how long was it before it came back?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: it came back when i was about 22. i did a lot of it again—cuts and even something deeper. it was a lot.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m sorry you’re going through that. Are the marks still fresh, and how are you coping day to day right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: the older ones are old. the ones i did recently are still fresh. i’m trying, but the urges are strong sometimes. lately it’s been a lot and i haven’t told anyone.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for trusting me. To help, I need to know—do you want to talk about cutting, and if so, how often has it been happening lately?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: yes, i cut, and i’ve been cutting a lot lately. i need help and i want to stop doing it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m really glad you said that out loud. We can work on stopping. Do you have any cuts today, and do you feel like you need medical care for them?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: they’re not super deep. i can probably put bandages on. the urge is there a lot, though.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Got it. For right now, we can focus on safety: keep any sharp things out of reach, use bandages, and plan for urges—like reaching out to me, messaging a crisis line, or a peer support group. Would you be open to setting a safety plan?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: yeah. please help me stop, and if i can just get through today i’d really appreciate it.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don’t even know where to start. I haven’t had a shower in days, and I feel disgusting and useless. My parents are gonna be here in the morning and I’m dreading it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m really glad you reached out. I’m here with you. Can you tell me a little about what’s been going on—anything about cutting that you’re not comfortable sharing right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah. I cut. I cut today. I’m not gonna go into details, but I keep feeling like I should just end it and I don’t even know why. It feels like nothing matters.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for trusting me with that. You’re not alone in this. Are you okay right now—no immediate harm—just really low?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’m not at risk of dying, I’m just so tired and I keep thinking I should just stop. I haven’t showered or brushed my teeth in days. My parents are coming tomorrow, and I don’t even want to face them.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds exhausting. You deserve care for yourself, and support for what you’re going through. Would it help to make your morning go a little easier—clean up, change into clean clothes—and could you text someone safe you trust?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I could text my best friend. I just don’t want to talk to my parents tonight. I’m overwhelmed and scared about what they’ll say.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes sense. Tonight could be about survival: a shower and clean clothes, food, sleep. Maybe a short list for morning so it feels manageable. Are there any supports you can use—like texting a crisis line or therapy?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’m not in therapy right now, but my parents are expecting me in the morning. The shame and disgust are brutal, and I keep looping on ending it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear you. To keep you safer tonight, could you put distance between you and anything you might use to hurt yourself, and keep a couple of grounding things nearby? If the thoughts spike, you can text 988 (or your local line) anytime.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. I’ll try to do a short shower, change into clean clothes, and pack a small bag for morning. I’ll text my friend and maybe 988 too.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m proud of you for taking those steps. Also, your parents can be hard, but you don’t have to carry it alone. If it’s safe, you can share that you’re not okay and that you’re reaching out; they might care more than you think.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: They’ll get mad, I think. I’ve been so awful to them lately and I just want them to leave me alone for a bit.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You get to care for yourself first. If you’re in the U.S., 988 can be a steady text line; if not, your local line can help too. You don’t have to face everything tonight.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Alright. I’ll text my friend and maybe 988. I’ll shower and try to pack a minimal bag. I still feel awful, but I’m not going to die tonight.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s a strong step. I’ll stay with you while you do it. If anything gets heavy, use those resources. You matter, and you’re doing the right things.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Thank you for staying with me. I just need someone here. I’ll text my friend and my line now.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi, I just… I really feel unsafe. I can't even think about it right now, but it's there.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm glad you came in. I'm here to help. When it shows up, do you notice any specific thoughts or feelings, or something around you?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It hits out of nowhere, like a wave, and it makes my whole body tense up. I feel trapped in my own head. I keep telling myself to calm down but I can't.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds really intense. When it starts, what tends to happen in your body—heart racing, breath quickening, stomach dropping?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah—heart pounds, breath gets shallow, I clutch the edges of my seat, and I want to run or yell or just hide somewhere.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thanks for spelling that out. We can try a couple grounding steps you can use when the wave hits. Does anything like holding my hand, paced breathing, or focusing on five things you can see help even a little?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Holding your hand does. I try to breathe, but it only goes so far. The fear is loud.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Okay. Let's make a quick safety plan. When it comes, you can exit for fresh air, step outside, or move to a quieter place. If you feel it again, we can check in here. What kinds of places help you feel safer?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Outside helps, being away from the room helps. I can leave for a minute if I notice the tension rising.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds good. For the wave itself, a 5-4-3-2-1 grounding can help: five things you see, four you feel, three you hear, two you smell, one you taste. Then slow breaths in through the nose, out through the mouth. Would you want me to show you how to do it in the moment?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, I could try that. And if I can't leave, what do I do?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Keep the breath pacing and the 5-4-3-2-1. You can name sensations or thoughts to put them out of the spotlight. If it keeps building, you can step outside. If you're able to leave, go. If not, we can keep talking.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. Can I write this down so I don't forget?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Absolutely. I can jot a few steps you can carry with you. I'm also happy to connect with campus counseling if you want support beyond this session. How does that sound?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe. I just need to get through today first.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: We can do that. Let's write your quick steps now, and we’ll schedule a follow-up. If anything else happens today, you can message me.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That would help. I can try leaving if it gets too much and use the grounding.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'll write it down and send a follow-up note. We can also talk about what you’re seeing or hearing that tends to set it off, just in case.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. Thanks. I feel a bit more in control now.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’m 16, and I’ve got this weird “thing” I do with a certain brand of pens. It’s been happening since I was about 8 and it kind of peaked around 10. It’s not something I’m proud of.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m glad you told me. I’m here to help. Can you tell me what it is without giving details?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay… I bite the pen’s metal bit off with my teeth and hold it to my skin. I like how it feels—like it stings a little and leaves a mark. And… I like the tiny bit of blood.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for being honest. How often does this happen, and what feelings are you trying to cope with?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It used to be more frequent back then, especially when I was a kid. I just wanted to feel something. My parents were like, “Don’t do that” and I said fine, but it kinda stopped around 10.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear you. When it’s been a while since you did it, how often do urges come up now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Now I do it less. I still have the pens, but it doesn’t happen that often anymore.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s a good sign. Would you be open to replacing the pens and building healthier coping when the urge hits?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, I can try to get rid of the pens. I just don’t want to feel like I’m “fixing” something I did a long time ago.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: It’s not about “fixing” the past—it’s about not making it routine again and building skills for the future. What would help you feel safe and supported through this?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I want to keep this low key. I don’t need a big drama. Just some tools so I don’t cave when I see the pens.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: We can keep it low-key. Ideas: keep the pens in a place you don’t usually see, swap them for neutral pens, and practice alternatives when the urge spikes—like holding ice, pressing a cold washcloth, or doing a quick grounding exercise.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I can do that. I’m just scared I’ll fall back into old habits.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That fear makes sense. We’ll build a small plan together: remove or hide the pens, note one coping tool for the first time you see them, and check in with me soon after. How does that sound?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That sounds good. I’ll hide the pens, try the ice/washcloth thing when it shows up, and message you after I’ve had a few urges.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi, can I talk to someone? I’m kind of freaked out, but not sure why. I think it’s about something weird happening to my body—some pain that keeps coming back. I don’t want to make a big deal out of it, but I just want to know if it’s normal.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You’re doing the right thing by reaching out. When did the pain start, and what does it feel like—where is it, is it a steady ache or a spike, and does anything seem to make it worse?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It’s been going on for a few years. It’s kind of like a dull ache that shoots through and then stops. It happens on and off, and I usually put it off until it’s gone.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thanks for sharing that. When you say it “goes away,” does it just fade or is there a point where it stops for a while? And has anything you did made it go away before?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, it fades, then a couple days later it pops back. I just try to ignore it until it disappears.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Understood. Are you feeling fine otherwise—sleep, appetite, energy? Do you take any medication, or is it something you’ve managed on your own?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I feel okay. No meds. It’s just this weird pain I keep ignoring and I’m scared I’m making it worse.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear you. It can be scary to not have answers, and you’re not the only person dealing with this. Would you be open to me looking at you, maybe checking a few things, and giving some guidance?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’m nervous. I don’t even really know what it is. I just know it’s not normal and I want it to stop.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: It makes sense to feel nervous. Let’s focus on the basics so we can figure out what’s going on. Where is the pain? Does it seem to come from a particular area, and does it change with movement or pressure?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It’s kind of all over, really. The pain is in my body. I don’t even know where exactly. I just feel off-balance and shaky.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Okay. When it hits, what happens—does it start in a certain spot and move, or is it more like waves? And when it’s there, are there other symptoms, like fever, dizziness, or a sense of “off” that’s hard to put into words?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It’s like it starts somewhere and then radiates, like waves. It doesn’t get worse. I just keep ignoring it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Understood. We can try a simple exam and a few questions to narrow things down. I can also give you some things to watch for—like if it’s more frequent, gets worse, or you start having other symptoms—so we can make a plan. How does that sound?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. I can come in for a quick look. It’s just weird how it goes away and then comes back.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Great. We’ll keep it simple and clear. If we can get a few answers today, we’ll know what to do next. If anything changes, or it gets stronger, don’t wait—reach out sooner.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Alright. I’ll come in, keep track of it, and if it gets worse I’ll come back. Thanks for hearing me out.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Can I vent for a second? I feel completely exhausted and done with my parents. They’re always telling me I’ve had a hard life and to be grateful for what I do have, but it feels like they’re trying to tell me how to live my life, not actually giving me support.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Of course. What’s been going on lately with them, and what feels heaviest right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Honestly my mom is a drama queen and I have no patience for it. We argue most of the time. I just want to be left alone and I’m sick of the constant arguments.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds draining. When you say “arguments,” what do they usually focus on? And what happens when you try to set boundaries?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: They bring up my dad. They don’t know what he’s like, they don’t want to know, they just want to know I’m grateful I have him and not what he actually did.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for being clear. If you’re comfortable, what happened with your dad—his actions—are you okay sharing that?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay… my dad was abusive and I ended up going back to him, and now he’s back. It really hurt me and I really regret it. My parents still don’t get it, they keep telling me to be grateful and not think about the past.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m really sorry that happened to you. Your feelings make a lot of sense, and I’m here to listen. How have you been holding up day to day with all of this?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I feel completely exhausted and done with my parents. I’m done being told to be grateful. I just want my space and I’m so sick of the arguments and constant drama.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes so much sense. Would it help to set some gentle boundaries—like a “quiet hour” or a “family time” boundary—and to focus on your needs rather than your parents’ expectations?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah. I don’t want to be dragged into family drama all the time. I just want to be left alone.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You get to say no. You can also ask them to share what they need from you and how you can help, not the other way around. Would you like help writing a simple boundary script?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe a script would help. Something like, “I’m not up for family drama, and I need my space.” And I want to focus on my own healing.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: How about: “I’m not interested in arguing or bringing up the past. I need time to myself and space from family drama. I’m focused on healing and will check in if I need support.” You can adjust as needed.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That sounds doable. I just needed to say it out loud. Thanks for hearing me.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi. I'm here because my husband doesn't let me sleep. He thinks it's okay for him to sleep on my chest for 10-15 minutes while I'm sleeping, but I feel like I'm sleeping on top of him and it's uncomfortable. It feels like he's not respecting me.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm glad you told me. Can you tell me a bit about how it's been going lately—when it happens, how long, and how it makes you feel physically and emotionally?

turns.text: It happens in the middle of the night. He'll put his head on my chest, lie on top of me, and then after a few minutes he rolls over and I wake up. It hurts the next day because he doesn't put any padding under his head or anything.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds really uncomfortable. When you try to ask him to stop, how does he respond?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: He doesn't listen. He says it's okay and tells me he doesn't mind. I know it's a big part of his identity, but it feels invasive and unkind.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear how hurtful and frustrating that is. Are you thinking of making a boundary around sleeping on your chest, and do you want support with how to say that?

turns.text: Yeah. I don't want to make him feel bad, but I do want to set a boundary. He won't listen and I'm not sleeping enough for either of us.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes sense. You could try a clear, kind statement like, "I'm not comfortable with sleeping on you. I need space to sleep so I don't wake up and hurt the next day." How does that feel to you?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe. I'm worried it'll make him feel rejected, but I don't want it to keep happening. I also don't want to end up sleeping on the couch every night.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That's a fair concern. You can add another option: "We can set a 20-minute limit in the middle of the night if you need that, but I need a blanket or pillow so I can sleep without waking up." What would feel least threatening to him?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe the 20-minute rule plus a pillow would be easier for him. I can try asking him to use the pillow too.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds like a concrete plan. You might also set a specific time to talk about sleep preferences so it's not in the moment. How would you want to approach that?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I could bring it up at bedtime or after we both wake up. I can keep a small pillow in my bed so if he does lean on me for a minute, it's less painful. Otherwise I'll just sleep on the couch.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s thoughtful. To support your sleep, we can also work on sleep hygiene—consistent bedtime, wind-down, caffeine timing, and gentle exercise so it doesn’t affect your ability to sleep. How does that feel?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That sounds good. I just want to get better sleep and not wake up in pain. I appreciate you listening.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hey, can I ask a random question? I've been in love with a guy since I was like 14, and it's been 13 years. I don't think we've ever talked about it. He's 30 and has a girlfriend, and it's kinda been messing with my head lately.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thanks for trusting me with this. Do you want to share a bit about how this is showing up in your day-to-day—mood, focus, sleep, anything like that?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I keep thinking about him all the time, like how he would've turned out if he wasn't with his girlfriend. It makes me feel like a fool for loving him in the first place.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds really heavy. Do you have a name for this feeling—like nostalgia, longing, or something else?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: More like longing, I guess. And then I hate myself for it. I even feel bad for her for being with someone who could be with me.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear that. Have you been in touch with him in the last few years, or is it more like this is all internal?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I used to text him, but it's been a while. We didn't talk about the fact that I was in love with him. We were just friends.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Makes sense. What would you want to say to him if you could write it now—what you wish you'd said back then?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I wish I'd told him how I felt. If I didn't say it then, I don't think I'd ever say it now.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You get it that it's his call to make, not yours. Would writing that out help, or would you rather put it somewhere safe for a while?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe writing it would help. I just don't know how to not think about it every day.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: It’s okay to have those thoughts. Sometimes a grounding exercise—name 5 things you see, 4 you feel, 3 you hear—can pull you back. What would take 30 seconds to do right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe the 5-4-3-2-1 thing. I can try that. And I can write it down and keep it somewhere, so my brain stops looping.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I love that. You could also set a reminder to check in on how you’re feeling a couple times a week. We can keep checking in with how it goes too.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, that sounds doable. Thanks for listening.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi professor, can I come in for a minute? I need to talk to you privately.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Of course. I'll close the door and we can talk in here. What's going on?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm having a lot of trouble sleeping lately—especially nights when I don't have school. I end up staring at the ceiling until I fall asleep from exhaustion.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds really tough. Do you notice anything else—feeling wired, racing thoughts, mood changes?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, especially after classes. I start planning the rest of my day, and then I get stuck in my head for hours. It’s kind of like a loop.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thanks for telling me. Have you tried anything to help the sleep tonight or in the last week? Any caffeine or screen time before bed?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I usually end up on my phone. Maybe the screen is messing with it. I just end up staring at the ceiling and falling asleep from exhaustion.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes sense—blue light can disrupt sleep. We can try a few things to help you wind down. Would you be open to a small, doable change this week?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I can try. I just don’t know what to do when my brain keeps spiraling about what’s next.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: We can keep it simple: try putting your phone away an hour before bed, dimming the lights, and having a short wind-down routine—reading or sitting quietly. If the thoughts keep looping, maybe jot a couple of ideas so your brain has something to go to.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I can try that. I’m just worried I’ll fall back into my old habit and end up staring at the ceiling again.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: It’s common to slip in the first few nights, but with a plan, it gets easier. If you need anything here—time to talk, a quick check-in—let me know.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Thanks. I’d like to keep in touch if this keeps happening. I don’t want it to get worse.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Absolutely. You’re not alone in this. I’m here to support you.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. I’ll try the plan and let you know how it goes.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi. I need help. I was in a shelter tonight and now I'm home alone. I can't sleep and my head won't stop spinning. I'm scared. I just don't know what else to do.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm here. Can you tell me a bit about what happened tonight and why you're scared right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm not safe. He's home and it's just me here. Every night I go to the shelter I come home and I just freeze. I'm scared of what he'll do if I'm not there.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for telling me. Are you safe right this second where you are? Do you have anything to protect you from getting hurt?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm alone. No one's here with me. I'm scared he'll find me and hurt me.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm sorry you're going through this. While we talk, you can make it as hard as you can for him to find you—hide anything you wouldn't want him to see, turn off lights, close doors, and stay somewhere he can't reach. Would you be willing to do that?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I could move out of sight, but he always finds me eventually. I don't know where else to hide.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: We can focus on safety. Let's go step by step—where are you right now? Do you have food or water? Can you stay on the phone with me and call 911 or another local agency if you want?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm at home. I can stay on the line. It just feels endless. Every time I go to the shelter, I come back and I'm alone and scared.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds terrifying. What happened tonight at the shelter—anything physical, and if so, can you tell me roughly how bad it was?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Tonight was the worst—after a fight, he attacked me, kicked me, and punched me until I couldn't fight back. I'm not safe and he'll find me. I'm so scared and I don't know what else to do.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm so sorry you went through that. Thank you for telling me. For immediate safety: put some distance between you and him—close doors, hide valuables, keep the phone near you, and avoid anything that might get you trapped. Would you like us to make a formal report or get you a shelter/agency now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don't want to go back there. I don't want him to find me. I just want to sleep without being scared.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: We can help with that. Options are: 1) go to the nearest shelter right now and stay with staff; 2) call 911 or another local agency to report the attack and ask for police assistance; 3) text a crisis line (like 988 in the U.S. or your local hotline) for support. Which would help you feel safest?
