turns.text: I stopped. It just keeps popping up and people keep saying I should feel guilty because I wasn't forced.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear that. Guilt can be a heavy weight. When those thoughts show up, what feels hardest about them?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It makes me feel dirty and weak. I hate that people make me feel that way for doing something I was trying to get rid of.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes sense. When you say you were trying to get rid of it, what was the original reason you started?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I felt stupid because I couldn't get rid of it, and I didn't even want to do it in the first place. It was an impulse that I didn't really feel like doing. I feel so bad about it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: An impulse doesn't define who you are. When it pops up again, how do you usually respond right now—do you try to suppress it?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Sometimes I try to ignore it. Other times I just freak out and overthink it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Let's try a gentler plan: first, give it space—name it without judgment. Then, a grounding anchor like slow breathing or a grounding statement. Would that feel doable?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I could try naming it. I just don't want to feel like I'm a bad person for wanting to feel better.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You're doing the right thing by wanting to heal. If you want, we can make a tiny plan for days when it shows up, and I can also help you address the guilt with people you feel judged by.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I like that. I want to stop feeling guilty. I just need a way to hold myself a little lighter.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: A simple script you can use when the judgment comes up: “I did something in the past that hurt me; it’s not who I am now. I’m here for healing.” How does that sound?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That sounds good. I can try saying it to myself and maybe to people I care about.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Good. You don't have to carry the guilt alone. If you want, we can also set up a small check-in so you're not alone in the healing.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I want to keep talking with you and try a plan for when it shows up again. Thank you for listening.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi, I'm here because I'm feeling really off lately and I'm not sure what to do. I've had a lot of stress lately, and I'm trying to figure out how to manage it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm glad you reached out. We can work through this together. Can you tell me what part is hitting you the hardest right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I just feel exhausted and on edge. My brain keeps spinning, and I'm not sure if I'm overreacting or if this is a sign of something bigger.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes a lot of sense. Sometimes when we carry a lot of stress over time, our bodies and thoughts respond in ways that feel extreme. Do you feel safe right now, and are there any changes in sleep, eating, or energy?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I feel safe physically. Nights are rough—sleep is spotty, and my anxiety spikes at the smallest things. I've been having trouble focusing on school and stuff with my mom and boyfriend.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thanks for that detail. When did these changes start, and what, if anything, happened around that time?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It started around my birthday—last year my birthday—when my ex raped me. I'm 17 now and that was over a year ago, but I feel like it was like yesterday and I still don't know if I'm going to be okay with it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm really sorry that happened to you. I'm glad you told me. You're not overreacting. What parts of it feel hardest for you day to day—emotions, thoughts, or body sensations?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It's like I'm stuck in a loop. I'm angry at him, angry at myself for letting it happen, and scared that I'm not going to be okay. I'm scared of what could happen, and I'm scared of what's already happened.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s a lot to carry. You deserve support. Are there any ways you’ve noticed it getting even slightly easier—small moments, music, a short walk, or talking with someone?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I tried music and walks a little. I don’t really talk much. I feel alone with it, like no one really gets it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: It’s not your fault to feel that. We can make it a bit steadier—consistent check-ins, simple routines, and small choices to reduce triggers. Would you be open to trying a daily plan that includes sleep, a check-in, and a short stress-reduction activity?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, I can try that. I just don't want to set something up for myself and then feel like it's not enough.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Totally. It’s about pacing: 20 minutes of gentle activity, a few minutes of a grounding check, and 15 minutes of something you like. How does that sound?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That sounds doable. I can start with that and see if it helps.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Good. We can also connect you with campus counseling to give your body and mind more support, and I’ll check in next week. How does that feel?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Feels okay. Thanks for listening.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don’t know what to even say. My head is spinning. I’m trying to get over the shock and the guilt about it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m really glad you came to talk. What’s feeling the heaviest right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: The shock, mostly. And the guilt—I just feel like this is my fault.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That guilt is common after something like this, but it doesn’t mean it’s your fault. What happened—can you share a little?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: My stepmom did some stuff with my father, and he wasn’t happy, so he got into it with me. I didn’t want to be involved, but I got dragged into it and had to get in the middle of their fight. I’m trying to get over that and it’s harder than I expected.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for trusting me with that. When you say you got dragged into it, what did that mean in those moments?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: My stepmom did things with my father, and he wasn’t happy. I was there, he got into a fight with me, and I’m trying to figure out how to handle that guilt now.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: When you say he got into a fight with you, did it involve physical violence? You can tell me anything you’re comfortable with.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: He did hit me. I was just 11. I don’t know how to let it go and stop blaming myself.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m really sorry that happened. None of that is your fault. It was a choice he made, and it hurts to go through that as a child.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: He hit me, and I didn’t want to be involved with him and my stepmom fighting. That was my stepmom’s husband, so I’m dealing with that. That’s the thing that’s stuck with me.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for saying that so clearly. Are you safe now? And what feels hardest about it—guilt, memories, your body?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’m safe now. I feel guilty and it’s hard to process. People say I don’t have to carry the blame, but I still feel like it’s my fault.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I get that—especially coming from 11. Blame can stick. Let’s try small steps: a safe space to talk, grounding tools, and naming what you feel in your body when memories show up.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That would help. I just don’t know where to start.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Good first step: pick one grounding exercise for a few minutes, write down the facts and feelings without judgment, and reach out to someone you trust. We can also connect you with resources for healing from past trauma. What would feel most doable right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: hi, sorry. i needed to reach out because i have some stuff that’s weighing on me.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m glad you reached out. What’s been feeling heaviest lately?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: a lot of stuff. i feel like i’m spiraling and i don’t know what to do.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds really tough. Are you feeling stuck with anything—work, school, personal stuff?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: yeah, it’s kind of everywhere. i’m stuck on what to do with my life, and i can’t get out of it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That feels overwhelming. Is there one area that feels more urgent—something small you could take one step on?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: not sure. i know i don’t want to be here in a few years if i’m still like this. i want to be better.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That desire to change is strong. Sometimes a tiny, repeatable action helps. Would you try one thing for this week?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: maybe. i’ve got so much to fix and i just keep spiraling.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That spiral makes sense when the load feels big. What if we pick the smallest thing—like a morning check-in or a short list? No pressure.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: i could write down what i’m stuck on and see what one thing feels doable, maybe.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s a solid start. Also, what helps you feel less overwhelmed when you’re stuck?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: a tiny routine and reminding myself not to fix everything at once. mostly just to start.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Great. For tonight, could you write the one tiny thing and then put it away for now? And then we check in here later?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: yeah, i can do that. i’ll jot it down and then take a break from it for now.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds like a strong plan. How would you like to check in—another quick note or a brief text?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: a quick note later would be fine. just need to remember not to keep spiraling.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’ll be here to listen. If the spiral feels stronger, you can also message me or use campus support; we’ll find what helps you.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: okay. thanks for listening. i’ll try the one step and reach out later.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You’re welcome. I’m proud of you for stepping up. You’re not alone in this, and you’re not stuck forever.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: thank you. i just needed someone to tell me that.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’ve been thinking of writing a poem about my friend’s funeral. What do you think about that idea?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s a beautiful idea. How are you feeling about writing it right now—comforted by the thought, or overwhelmed?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’m trying to be okay, but I keep thinking about how hard it will be to say goodbye and how it feels like my friend’s leaving will never stop.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes sense. Would a short, heartfelt poem help capture the feelings—what parts feel most important to include?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I want to keep it honest and touching. I don’t want to make it too cheesy.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That balance is tough. Maybe focus on specific moments—what they shared, what they liked to do, or what they said last.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I like that. I want it to feel like a tribute that still honors them for who they are. Any advice on tone?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Warm and sincere. Maybe a quiet, steady rhythm—not too fast or slow.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I could try that. I’m not sure I want to read it in front of people, just write it and keep it close.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Totally understandable. Maybe write it in a quiet space so it feels like the right place for you.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I think I’ll keep it short. Something like “A small farewell poem for a friend.” Is that a good title?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s honest and clear. If you want, we can try a few lines and I can give feedback.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. Here’s what I’ve got: “I will miss you, friend. Your laughter echoes in my head, your warmth still surrounds me. I know you’re not here anymore, but I keep remembering you.”

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s really good. You’ve captured presence and absence. Maybe add one more line to ground it or offer comfort.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe something like, “I carry you in memories—your kindness, your jokes, how you loved life.”

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That works well. It’s concise, genuine, and leaves a lasting impression. If it feels right, you can print it to carry.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, I think that’s enough. I’ll make a clean draft and keep it private for now.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m glad. You’ll have something real to hold onto. When you’re ready, it can be a quiet way to honor them.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Thank you. It helps to have someone look at it.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi, I’m kind of nervous. I came because it got really heavy last week and I don’t know how to stop.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m glad you came. Let’s take it one step at a time. What’s been feeling the heaviest lately—sleep, school, friends, or something else?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Mostly sleep. I toss and turn most nights, my brain won’t quiet down, and I feel more exhausted than I used to when I’m not up all night.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds really draining. When you’re up late, what’s going on in your head—worrying, replaying the past day, planning for tomorrow, or something else?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It’s the past day and the next day, the past day and the next day… and I feel like it’s going to keep getting heavier and worse.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for being honest. When you say "heavier," are you talking about thoughts about not wanting to be here, or is it more about everything just piling up?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’ve been having thoughts about killing myself lately, and they’re getting more frequent and heavier. It’s been going on for a little over a week.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m really glad you told me directly. Are you safe right now, and do you have any plan to act on those thoughts today?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’m safe. No plan—just heavy thoughts. Nights are the worst because my brain won’t stop looping.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thanks for clarifying. Let’s aim for safety first: can you keep the environment around you, and is there anyone you can message or call right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I can keep the space around me and text someone. I mostly need help stopping the loop.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Okay. We can try a short nighttime routine: put on a show you like, dim the lights, maybe a warm shower before bed, and if thoughts spike, pause and text the person you set up. How does that feel?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That could help. I can try a show and a shower, and I’ll text them if it spikes.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Also, maybe keep it small tonight—no heavy work or decisions. When you’re alone, try a couple grounding steps, and reach out to the person you’ll text. Would you be open to texting me too?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah. I can try grounding and check in with you if it gets rough. I’ll text that person too.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m here to help. If it feels safe, a brief phone call or text anytime. We’ll check in again next session. For tonight, focus on safety, a simple wind-down, and reach out if the thoughts get heavier.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I need help. I've been cutting myself so hard my skin is splitting and my body looks worse. I'm in pain and I don't think I can do this much longer.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm really glad you told me. Are you hurting right now, and do you have any open wounds or injuries needing medical attention? I can't help with anything that harms you—please stay safe while we talk.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I've been cutting so hard my skin is splitting. I keep doing it and it keeps getting worse. I'm in pain and I don't think I can take it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm so sorry you're going through this. Thank you for being honest. Are you alone right now, and are you having any thoughts about not wanting to be here?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah… I've been cutting so hard my skin is splitting. I keep doing it and it keeps getting worse. I'm in pain and I don't think I can do this much longer. I don't want to be here anymore.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm really glad you said that out loud. We can work on keeping you safe and getting you some support. Right now, would you be willing to put distance between you and anything you could use to hurt yourself, and stay with me here while we take the next steps?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I just feel like there's no point in continuing. I keep doing it and it gets worse, and then I feel more broken.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds unbearable. I care about your safety. Can you move whatever you’re using and put some distance between you and anything that could hurt you? Are you able to sit with me while we focus on getting you support and pain relief?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I can move it. I just hate how bad it looks now and how much it hurts. I want to stop but it keeps getting worse.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you. While we talk, could you keep your wounds clean and loosely covered, and keep your hands away from anything you use? If it feels like you might act on those thoughts, would you be willing to text 988 or stay on a video call with me and a counselor?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I can text. I'm alone and it's loud and I feel like it's getting louder. I need this to stop.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm here with you. While we wait for help, could you make one small shift to lower your risk—set something on your phone and sit next to it, or step away from anything you could use? I’ll stay with you and check in with you.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay, I can set something on my phone and sit by it. I just want this to stop and my body to stop hurting.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds like a strong step. If the thoughts intensify or you feel like you need emergency care, text 988. We can also plan for support after this—would you be open to a follow-up with a counselor or therapist?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, I can text. I still hate how bad it looks and how much it hurts, but I can try texting.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s enough for now. Keep your wounds clean and covered, stay in the space next to your phone, and stay safe. If you need anything or it gets worse, call or text 988. I'm here with you.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. I'm staying here and texting. Please keep talking with me.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi. I need to report something that’s been bothering me about my coworker.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m glad you came in. We’ll go at your pace. What’s been happening?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It’s about the office printer we use in the common area. She keeps telling me it won’t print unless I load a sheet, then when she prints the same file later she can do it with no sheets. I don’t know if she’s lying, lying about what she said, or just confused.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s a lot to juggle. When she says that, are there witnesses or anything she said in writing?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don’t remember any written statements. I’ve just had a lot of back-and-forth with her, and now I don’t even trust myself anymore.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Understood. If it’s in the common area, it could affect multiple people. When you say she loads a sheet, do you mean a single sheet, or multiple, and what exactly happens?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Single sheet. She loads one sheet, then it works. When she later prints the same thing, she can do it with no sheets. She’s told me it’s a technical issue that only she knows how to fix.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for being specific. If she’s making you do that, we can document and stop the pattern. If you don’t have witnesses or documentation, we can still note the pattern and ask that you don’t take action without checking first. Would you like that approach?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah. I don’t want to keep doing it without checking.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Okay. We’ll record the pattern and ask that you inform the facility manager before doing anything to the printer. Do you have permission to do that?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’m okay with telling the facility manager. I just don’t want to end up in a situation where I keep doing the wrong thing.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes sense. Before you do anything, ask the manager. If she wants you to add sheets, you can say you’ll inform her. For now, stop the behavior unless you have permission, and document this with the manager and HR.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Got it. I can document this, stop without sheets, and tell the manager next time.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Good plan. We’ll take a note and keep it on file, then follow up after your manager speaks with the facility team. If you want, we can also discuss how to handle any verbal pressure from her.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That would help. I just want it to stop.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don't even know why I'm posting. This feels embarrassing, but I just wanted to say something that's been with me for a while.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You're not alone in feeling that way. I'm here to listen. What happened, and how are you doing right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: About a month ago I cut my arm with a straight razor and I was fine for 3 days, then 2 weeks later it flared up again.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm glad you came here. Do you still have the wound today? Are you feeling okay right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Still there, just more of a line. I'm fine, I swear. But it's been bugging me this whole time.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thanks for being honest. We can take care of you here. Would you be willing to share what led up to the first time, or what's been making you feel this way recently?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: A little over a month ago I started self-harming, I cut my arm with a straight razor and it took a few days to heal and then a couple weeks later it flared again.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for trusting me with that. I'm really glad you told me. Are you having any pain, redness, pus, or fever? Is the wound still open and clean?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: No fever, not really painful, it just looks like a line and I'm just really embarrassed about it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear you. We can take care of the wound, and I also want to support you through the pain that led to this. Would you be open to a follow-up check for safety and referrals?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, please. I don't want to do it again, and I feel weird about it and also relieved it's over.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That mixed feeling makes sense. Let's go step by step: wound care, cleaning if it needs it, and then we can discuss safety supports. Are there any triggers or times that make it harder?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It's just been there for weeks and I haven't had the urge to do it again.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Okay. We can dress it today and schedule a follow-up to make sure it's healing. If you want, I can connect you with counseling on campus.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Please. I don't want it to flare again.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm glad you're here. We'll care for the wound and start a plan. We'll also talk about staying connected and getting the help you need.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Thanks. I'm just glad I didn't go all the way.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’ve never had a good relationship with my dad. We never got along, and now he’s in the hospital with cancer—what do I do? I don’t even know where he is.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m really sorry you’re dealing with this. Are you close enough to a hospital to visit, or are you planning to call someone in person?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’m not close. It’s not even my hospital; I don’t know where he is. I’m not even sure if I should go.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s understandable. If you can, ask someone you trust—like a friend, family member, or your own family—to check in and maybe arrange a visit for you. You can also look up the hospital’s visitor policy to get info on visiting hours and requirements.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I could try. I’m worried I’ll mess up and say the wrong thing. I don’t want to say anything that makes him upset.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Totally fair. If you go, a simple, kind presence can mean a lot. Let him know you’re thinking of him, maybe offer to bring a small gift or some tea from home, and keep the tone gentle and open. If you’re nervous, you could write a short note you’ll read or hand him.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I do care. It just hurts that our relationship was so bad and now this is happening. I don’t want it to feel like the last time I see him.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You don’t have to fix anything right now. You can bring comfort, not a performance. If distance makes it hard, you can still call him and just say you’re thinking of him, even if it’s brief.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’m not sure I’ll have the energy to go, but I wanted to ask what’s the right thing to do.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: The right thing is whatever feels doable and kind to you. If you’re really unsure, it’s okay to sit with a friend or a family member, or not go at all—then you can check in again later or send a letter.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That makes sense. If I do go, what should I say? I don’t want to make him uncomfortable.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Short and warm: “I’m thinking about you. You’re in my thoughts. If you want to talk, I’m here. If not, I’ll just sit with you.” If he wants, you could ask what he wants to talk about, or just bring a book or tea and listen.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I could try that. I just wish there was a clear “I should go” or “I shouldn’t.”

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You don’t have to decide right now. If you’re physically able and it feels right, a short visit or a call can count. If not, it’s okay to skip and check in later or send a letter—any connection is meaningful.

turns.text: Your safety is our top priority. Would it be okay if I share what steps we can take and maybe connect you with advocates who can support you while we talk to the investigator?

turns.speaker: User

turns.text: I hear how anxious that is. If you want to, we can talk through what to say and how to handle interactions. When you're ready, you can also decide what you want—full disclosure or keeping it to yourself—without judgment.

turns.speaker: User

turns.text: Honestly, I keep thinking about ending it all—like, I wish I didn't have to carry this around anymore—but I don't actually want to do anything about it right now.

turns.text: Thank you for being honest. I'm glad you're here talking. Right now, are you safe—no plans to act on those thoughts—and are you physically okay?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That background noise can get loud, but we can make it quieter, one small step at a time. Would you want to try a tiny plan for tonight—like setting one small task, a short break, or reaching out to someone?

turns.text: Yeah, that could help. I just need a little reminder that I'm not done and that this can get easier.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds incredibly exhausting. Does it show up a lot in school? Like in assignments, class, or homework? And what are the biggest “little mistakes” that hit hardest?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah in school a lot. A typo in a paper or a missed deadline makes me spiral. I feel stupid, like I’m not good enough. And I feel invisible. Like no one cares if I mess up.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes total sense. When the pressure spikes, how do you usually cope—do you try to fix it all by yourself, or would talking with someone help? Do you have anyone you trust to check in with?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I usually try to fix it myself. I don’t really tell people about my perfection panic, and I’m not great at asking for help. It’s more like “I suck and no one likes me.”

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You deserve help, not judgment. Maybe we can build a tiny plan that lowers the bar a bit without letting you off the hook: realistic timelines, one small task at a time, and a small support check-in. Would you be open to that?

turns.speaker: User

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: We can make it concrete. Try picking one small thing (like a 10-minute assignment block) and set a gentle due date a day or two later. If you notice a typo, just fix it and keep going—no shame. Also, what would help you feel less invisible in the moment?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don’t know. I just feel like I’m not good enough. A typo feels like the end of the world.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Totally fair. A typo is an edit, not a judgment on your worth. Would you consider jotting a “tiny win” list after each small task—proof you did work? And if you could tell someone one thing without over-sharing, what might that be?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I could try a tiny win list. Telling someone might be hard, but maybe I can tell a friend or a teacher that I’m struggling.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s a great start. For this week: one small task, a gentle timeline, a small check-in with a teacher or friend, and a simple “win” after. Want me to help draft a message or set a reminder for you?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, a draft would help. And a reminder would be nice too. And just to be clear, I’m not “faking.” I really feel this.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear you. We can draft a short message like, “I’m working on a small assignment and I want to keep it simple. I need support with X if I can ask.” I’ll send the draft and set a gentle follow-up. For now, what’s one tiny step you’ll try today?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’ll do one small task today and just try not to blow it out of proportion. I’ll draft the message and see.

turns.speaker: User

turns.text: That sounds like a solid plan. If you want, I can help you keep a small journal so you can note what helped, and we can revisit here next week to check in. How does that sound?

turns.speaker: User

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m here for you. If you ever want to talk or just have a safe person to vent to, we can set up regular check-ins or find a peer group that shares similar interests.

turns.speaker: User

turns.text: That sounds okay. I'll take the referral, follow your steps, and try to get back to you if anything changes.

turns.speaker: User

turns.text: I can do that. I just need it to stop. I'm not doing anything today.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi. I need someone to talk to—like, really talk—because I’m spiraling and I don’t have anyone else I can say this to.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I’m really sorry you’re carrying that. You’re not broken for feeling this way. What does it feel like when they say that to you?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It’s like the whole damn family’s like, “We don’t even want you to be like your brother.” I feel worthless, like they’re always pointing out how much more he is than me. He’s an adult now, I’m still a kid, and they still treat me like I’m not doing anything right.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds incredibly hurtful. When they compare you to him, do they ever acknowledge what you are actually doing, or does it feel like it’s ignored?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: They just keep saying I’m not making a life out of it and I hate how they act, but I hate them. I want to tell them that their brother’s already in the army, and I’m still a kid, and I don’t want to be like him. How do I even say that out loud?

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You’re not obligated to say anything to them. You deserve compassion, not comparison. You could write it out to yourself so it feels real, then decide whether to say it to them, to friends, or to a counselor. Which feels safer right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don’t have anyone to talk to. I’m spiraling and I don’t know what to do. They’re always in my face about it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Let’s make a small plan to calm the spiral. Could you try: 1) write what you want to say to them (no pressure to send it), 2) take a short walk or do a grounding exercise, 3) check in with a trusted person or a hotline if you can, and 4) reach out to a counselor if school allows?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I think I could write it out and breathe. I just hate that they’re always doing that stuff to me.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear you. Would it help to practice one calm phrase you’d say back, like “I’m not doing this to please him—I’m doing it for myself,” and repeat it while you breathe or walk?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe. I can try that. I just want to not feel like I’m not living my life.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You are living your life, just not to the script they’ve set. Keep choosing yourself one small step at a time. If this is school-related, I can check for support options or help you reach out safely.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Thanks. I needed to vent and remember I’m not wrong for hating them.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I just feel so alone. I don't know what to do with myself anymore. I think I'm going mad and I don't have anyone to lean on. The loneliness is crushing and it doesn't even feel real, like the world is just moving on and I'm stuck here.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds incredibly painful. What's been happening day to day that makes it feel this heavy, and what part of it feels most hopeless right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Honestly, it's been like this for forever. Every day it feels the same. The loneliness is like a fog. I'm tired of fighting and I want this to be done so I can sleep.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for saying that. When you say "done," do you mean something specific about your day or life, or are you talking about ending your life?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It's that "done" thing. I just keep wishing I could disappear and never feel this again. I don't even know what it's called anymore.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm really glad you told me. You're not alone in this—people care and can help you get through it. Are you thinking about ending your life, or do you feel like you'd be ending it?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don't have the will. I don't have the strength. I'm just so tired. I wish I could disappear and just sleep, but I don't know how to make that happen.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: When you say you want to disappear, are you thinking about dying or not wanting to be here? Either way, you deserve support. Would it help if I stayed on with you, or if I could recommend some support lines or resources?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Honestly I don't even know what words to use. The wish is there, but I don't have the energy to do it. I'm just exhausted.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes sense. To be clear—what you're describing is a serious risk. Are you considering ending your life, or are you wishing it so hard that it feels like it would be easiest if you could just "not be here"?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I wish I could die. I'm not planning anything—I just don't want to be here anymore.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for being honest with me. I'm really glad you're talking. Right now, we can focus on getting you through tonight. Would you be open to texting 988 (in the U.S.) or your local crisis text line—"text HOME" to 988—and I can stay with you while you do that?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don't know. My family would never know what's wrong with me, and I don't have anyone to lean on. It feels like the world is moving on and I'm just stuck.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm here with you. Even if you don't share it with your family, you can still use 988. You don't have to be alone in this. Could you try messaging them right now while we sit here and you breathe?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay… let me try. I'll text "text HOME" and see if anyone answers. I just want to feel a little less alone tonight.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi. Can I tell you something that's been messing with me?

turns.text: Of course. I'm listening. What's been going on?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I keep thinking about how I'm not doing anything to change my life—like working, getting a real job, saving money, anything. I feel like I'm just stuck in a loop.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds really heavy. How long have these thoughts been around, and what makes them show up most?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It's like this constant background noise. My brain just keeps telling me I'm going to die and I'll be in a worse place if I'm in debt. It's like a loop I can't escape.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear that fear and the stuckness. Are you feeling safe right now, and do you have anyone you can reach out to for support?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm planning to kill myself soon. I'm tired of the debt and the loop, and I don't see a way out.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm really glad you told me. I'm sorry you're hurting. Are you in immediate danger right now, and do you have any means to hurt yourself nearby? You matter, and you can get help today.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm safe, just in a really bad place. I don't have anything right now. I keep thinking about the debt and how I'll be in a worse place if I'm in debt.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for telling me. Would you be willing to text or call someone you trust or a crisis line so you don't have to ride this alone tonight?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I don't know. I don't have anyone and I'm too scared to call.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That makes a lot of sense. If you'd rather not call, you can text a crisis line or use a chat line like 988 (US) or your local service—no pressure. You can also message me or keep talking here. While you do that, could you move away from anything that could be used to hurt yourself and put some distance between you and it?

turns.text: I can try not to think about it right now. I'll move away and keep talking.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds like a helpful first step. While you're waiting for help to arrive or while the support line is with you, try grounding—name five things you see, four you feel, three you hear, two you smell, one you taste.

turns.text: Okay. I can try that. I don't want to relapse though.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: It's okay to relapse sometimes—what matters is you're reaching out. If the thoughts spike, try a quick grounding loop and then connect again. You're not alone in this.
